Pradhip Das alias Shambhu and others ------- Judgment-debtor-Appellants.
Vs.

full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed C.J.: In this appeal by special leave the question is whether, on the death of a monthly tenant judgment-debtor, his heirs can be substituted for the purpose of execution of the decree for ejectment. In order words, whether a monthly tenancy is heritable. In an earlier decision of this Court in the case of Abdus Sattar Vs. Suresh Chandra Das, 32 DLR (171, which was followed in the case of Abdul Latif Vs. Abdul Mannan 1982 BCR, AD, 428, it was held by this Court that a monthly tenancy was not heritable and that the right of a monthly tenant in respect of a premises was his personal right which ceased on his death. Facts leading to this question are given below. 

 2. Respondents-landlords filed Other Suit No.172 of 1976 in the First Court of Munsif, Chittagong for ejectment of their monthly tenant, Sukhendu Bikash Das, on the ground of default in the payment of rent and also of bonafide requirement of the premises by them. The suit was decreed and the decree was upheld upto the High Court Division and thereafter the decree was put into execution by filing Execution Case No. 23 of 1984 against the tenant-judgment-debtor. During the pendency of the Execution Proceeding, the tenant, Sukhendu Das, died whereupon his heirs, who are appellants before us, were substituted. But they challenged the continuation of the Execution Proceeding by an application under section 151 of the Civil PC alleging that the tenancy created in favour of their predecessor, Sukhendu Das, ceased to exist on his death as it was his personal right and, as such, the decree against him became infructuous. Their contention was upheld by the learned Munsif who further held that for ejectment of the appellants a fresh suit was to be filed. But in revision, CR No.131 of 1985, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, held that the decree passed against the original tenant during his life time was perfectly valid and did not become infructuous and further that his heirs, though they did not inherit the tenancy right, were not trespassers either, but they became "tenants by sufferance". The Execution Proceeding was therefore held maintainable. Both the learned Single Judge and the learned Munsif sought support for their respective views from the decision of this Court in the earlier case of Abdus Sattar Vs. Suresh Chandra Das, 32 DLR (AD) 171 as referred to above. 

 3. Mr. SR Pal, learned Counsel, has appeared for the appellants in this case. He has submitted, though half-heartedly, that in view of the decision in the 32 DLR (AD) 171, the relationship of landlord and tenant in this case snapped on the death of the original tenant, Sukhendu Das, that his heirs did not inherit the tenancy and as such they could not have been substituted in the execution proceeding as the tenancy in favour of Sukhendu Das was a personal right which "is not heritable". The learned Counsel has, however, expressed serious doubt about the correctness of the decision in the 32 DLR (AD) 171 case and has submitted that if contention of the appellants in this case is rejected and decision of the learned Single Judge is upheld, the decision of this Court in 32 DLR (AD) 171 that the right of a monthly tenant is not heritable cannot but be reviewed and reconsidered. 

 4. In the earlier case, Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel had appeared for the appellant-landlord, and submitted that a monthly tenancy was heritable. To assist the Court Mr. SR Pal was engaged as amicus curiae in that ease. After hearing both Mr. Mahbubuddin Ahmed and Mr. SR Pal in that case, this Court rejected Mr. Mahbubuddin Ahmed's contention and held as stated above. In the instant case, Mr. SR Pal his appeared for the appellants-tenants; he has relied upon 32 DLR (AD) 171 decision in the different context. We engaged Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed as amicus curiae in this case. On behalf of the respondents-landlords Mr. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record has appeared to defend the decision of the High Court Division that the Execution Proceeding is quite maintainable. 

 5. As appears, the question before us in this appeal is a question of great public importance. Both Mr. SR Pal and Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed cited before us a great number of decisions including some decisions from the Indian jurisdiction. Mr. Pal, though he defends the High Court Division's decision in this case, has expressed the view that the earlier decision of this Court is not correct and that it has created serious complications in the landlord-tenant relation in respect of monthly tenants. Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed has reiterated his earlier stand that the right of a monthly tenant is heritable and that the earlier decision of this Court was not based on correct interpretation of Sections 105 and 106 of the Transfer of Property Act governing "lease of immovable property". Both the learned Counsels have contended that the earlier decision of this Court had resulted from an erroneous view that a lease under section 105, TP Act is quite different from a lease under section 106 of that Act. They contend that a tenancy, whatever may be its duration, is a "lease" and that the right of the tenant is not a personal right but it is survived by, and passes on, to his "legal representatives", as defined in the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 and also within the meaning of section 2(11) of the CP Code. In a nutshell, the decision in the previous case, in their opinion, needs to be reconsidered. 

 "106. In the absence of a contract or local law or usage to the contrary, a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes shall be deemed to be a lease from year to year, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by six months' notice expiring with the end of a year of the tenancy; and a lease of immovable property for any other purpose shall be deemed to be a lease from month to month, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by fifteen days' notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy " (relevant portion only) 

 This section provides that in the absence of a contract (or local law or usage), a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes "shall be deemed to be" a lease from year to year; and a lease for any other purpose, say for residential purpose, "shall be deemed to be" a lease from "month to month". It is here from which the term 'monthly tenancy' is derived. At to termination of these two kinds of leases, one from "year to year" and the other "from month to month", it has been provided in this section that in the case of the former, it is terminable by six months' notice expiring with the end of the year of the tenancy, and in the case of the latter, it is terminable by fifteen days' notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy. On careful consideration of these sections, we find that a 'lease', whatever may be its purpose or duration, is created only under section 105. This section does not say that a lease for an agricultural or manufacturing purpose shall always be a lease from year to year, or a lease for any other purpose shall always be a lease from month to month. In this section a legal fiction has been introduced in the words, "shall be deemed to be", just to fill up the vacuum left in the contract if any, or when there is no contract creating the lease, as to duration of the lease and the manner of its termination. As to a tenancy from month to month, it is provided, it shall be deemed to be terminable by fifteen days notice. This does not necessarily mean that its duration is only one month and that on the expiry of one month it shall cease to exist. A monthly tenancy, if provided in the contract, may continue for months or years together unless it is determined by a notice to quit under this section. In the case of monthly tenancy, the period of which has been fixed in the contract, it shall continue till the expiration of that period which may be one month or one year or several years. Similarly, the period of notice to quit may also vary in terms of the contract, such as, if the contract fixes the period of notice, say, two months, then notice of fifteen days will not be valid. 

 8. Section 111, TP Act, shows different ways and grounds for determination of a lease. One of the grounds for determination of a lease is "efflux of time limited thereby". That is, the period of the lease stated in the lease-agreement has expired. This means that if the period of a lease is fixed by the contract, written or creating the lease, then the lease shall stand terminated on the expiry of this period. Another way of determination of a lease is by serving a notice to quit upon the lessee by the lessor. This provision comes into play when no definite period has been fixed in the contract creating the lease. A lease may also be determined by voluntary surrender of the property to the lessor by the lessee. It may be noted that "death" of the lessee has not been mentioned in this section as a ground for determination of a lease. 

 9. In the previous decision of this Court 132 DLR (AD) 171], a clear distinction was made between a lease under section 105 and a lease under section 106 of the TP Act; whereas, these two sections do not appear to say so. In that decision a lease under section 105 was held to be a right in an immovable property but not so a lease under section 106. Upon consideration of section 105 it was observed in para 11 of that decision : "The lease, as defined, no doubt creates an interest in immovable property and the Act also says that it is transferable" We are to see the true character of the lease created under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act." It was further observed in para 13; "Analysing in this way, we find that a relationship is created under this section between the landlord and the tenant which is of a personal nature. The right of occupation of the premises has been given, and this right of occupation from month to month, from its very nature, cannot but be personal and so cannot create an interest in the land as a lease under section 105 does. The right of occupation remains personal with the tenant. The right being personal it ceases with the death of either party and so on the death of the tenant, the tenancy ceases and hence it is not heritable". 

 10. The Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963, in section 2(8), defines "tenant" which expression includes his "legal representative" "as defined in the Civil Procedure Code". A tenant under the Premises Rent Control Ordinance means "any person by whom, or on whose account, rent is payable for any premises and includes a legal representative as defined in the Civil Procedure Code". Furthermore, a person continuing in possession after the termination of a tenancy is also a tenant under this definition. A "legal representative" within the meaning of section 2(11) of the Civil PC means "a person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person, and includes any person who intermeddles with the estate of the deceased and where a party sues or is sued in a representative character the person on whom the estate devolves on the death of the party so suing or sued". A tenant under the Ordinance is same as a lessee under the TP Act and the monthly tenancy is also a lease within the meaning of section 105 TP Act. 'Tenancy' has not been defined in the Ordinance, but it clearly falls within "lease" as described in section 105 TP Act. "Tenancy" relates to "premises" which has been defined in the Ordinance". "Premises" means any building/hut or its part to be left for residential or non-residential purpose and includes garden, out-house and also furniture supplied by landlord. Whereas, lease 'covers all immovable property including a premises'. A legal representative of a person is one who represents his estate on his death. The lease under section 105 TP Act is transfer of a right to enjoy an immovable property. This right to enjoy, by occupation of a premises, which is no doubt an immovable property, is a limited right. Premises Rent Control Ordinance is intended to govern some specific aspects of a monthly tenancy, such as, the procedure for determination of a tenancy, for protecting tenant against unjust or improper eviction and prohibition of increase in the rent by undue means. Section 18 of the Ordinance is relevant for this purpose. Provision of this section shall prevail "notwithstanding anything contained in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 or the Contract Act, 1872". The provision is that no order or decree for recovery of possession of a premises shall be made as long as the tenant pays rent in full and regularly and performs all other conditions of the tenancy. In the previous decision the definition of "legal representative" of a tenant was of course looked into, but it was observed in para 8 that "the definition was inserted in the Ordinance only to emphasize the tenant's liability to pay rent and nothing more and this meaning becomes clear when we advert to the second half of the definition of 'tenant' which says that it also includes a person continuing in possession after the termination of the tenancy". We find it rather difficult to accept this view as correct that 'legal representative' of a deceased tenant will be brought to the scene only to pay rent and not to inherit the deceased tenant's right to hold the tenancy for the purpose of enjoying or occupying the premises. 

 11. A monthly tenancy being a lease within the meaning of section 105, TP Act, it is an interest in an immovable property. It is transfer of an interest in the property as shown in this section. The TP Act does not specifically say that a lease is heritable also, because this Act is not intended to govern the matter of succession to immovable property. But the incidence of heritability is easily discernible from the tenancy being an interest in the property. It is also easily gathered from the fact that a contract, which creates a tenancy is binding upon the parties to the contract as well as upon their heirs, and that, a contract is legally enforceable against parties thereto and their heirs. A tenancy may be created under a statute also; such as, on legal termination of a tenancy, a person continuing in possession and paying rent to the landlord, who accepts it, becomes a statutory tenant. In the instant case, we are not dealing with any statutory tenant. The tenancy in this case is a contractual tenancy. Right in such a tenancy is ordinarily heritable, though this right is limited "to enjoy" and occupy the property only, and the tenant is liable to be ejected either on the expiration of the fixed period, if any, or by notice to quit. 

 12. A number of cases from Indian jurisdiction have been cited before us in order to support the view that a monthly tenancy is heritable though right in the tenancy is limited or partial and the tenant inherits only that right which the original tenant held and nothing more. Among others, the following cases have been considered by us: Rajib Hossain and another Vs. Nowab Unus Khan, AIR 1937 Nagpur, 321; Anwar Ali Bepari Vs. Janakilal Roy Chowdhury, 43 CWN, 797; Smt. Vishnawati Vs. BV Chowdhury, AIR 1970, All. 389; Sau Nakabai Vs. Mahadu Sakharam Adsule and others, AIR 1980 Bom. 208. The then Dhaka High Court also held this view in the case of Gouribala Pal Vs. Kunjalal Saha, 12 DLR 37. The Indian Supreme Court, in the case of Damadilal and others Vs. Parashram and others, AIR 1976 (SC) 2229 considered the question as to heritability of a in contract. There is no dispute that a contractual tenant has an estate or property in the subject-matter of the tenancy and heritability is an incident of the tenancy. It cannot be assumed, however, that with the determination of the tenancy the estate must necessarily disappear and the statute can only preserve his status of irremovability and not the estate he had in the premises in his occupation". 

 13. That a tenancy is an interest in an immovable property was considered from another angle in a Letters-Patent appeal in the case of Ramchandra Annappa Vs. Subraya Timmaya, AIR 1951 Boni. 127. The question there was whether "tenancy right is protected under section 53A of the TP Act." It was contended that the tenancy being merely a transfer of a "partial right in property" viz a right to enjoy the property, it could not be said to be a transfer of property within the meaning of the expression used in section 53A of TP Act. The contention was rejected and it was held that though the right is only to enjoy the property still it is a right and the tenancy is a transfer of immovable property within the meaning of section 53A of the TP Act. 

 14. This Court in the previous decision (32 DLR (AD) 171) took into consideration two concepts of English law of tenancy to support the view that a monthly tenancy creates only "personal right" of the tenant which vanishes with his death. One of the concepts is "tenancy-at-will". Such a tenancy under the English law is created and continues at the mere will of the landlord; it is terminable at any time, without any notice, at the mere will of the landlord; it is also terminable at any time, without any notice at the wish of the tenant. The relation between landlord and tenant under this concept of tenancy is a personal relation between the two and is terminable by the death of either of them. From this point of view, this Court came to the conclusion that a tenancy from month to month is in the nature of the English tenancy of "tenancy-at-will". In our law governing tenancy there is no such concept as "tenancy-at-will" to be terminable at any time and without any notice at the mere wish of either party. Under our law a person may get possessory right in an immovable property by a licence granted by the owner of such property. Such a right is terminable, at any time, at the mere will of the person granting the licence. The person who is granted this right is Galled a "licensee". A licensee is not a tenant; but a tenant from month to month under TP Act is different from a licensee. Taking them at par is found to have led to the erroneous view that a monthly tenant is same as a "tenant-at-will". A tenancy from month to month, as we have already found, dots not mean that it is meant for only one month, at the end of which it ceases to exist, and thereupon, a fresh tenancy is to start. Similar view was taken in the case of Usha Rani Devi Vs. The Research Industries Ltd., 50 CWN, 461. There it has been held that a monthly tenancy is not a tenancy which commences or begins in one month, and on the expiry, a fresh tenancy is created in the following month or months, but is a tenancy for an unstated period, which is, however, determinable by either party by a notice to quit. 

 15. The other English concept, as considered by this Court in the earlier case, is "tenant by sufferance". A tenancy created by sufferance comes into being when, on the lawful termination of a tenancy, the landlord by his own act of negligence, does not take steps to enforce his right of evicting the tenant who therefore continues in possession by landlord's negative permission. Such a tenant by "sufferance" acquires no right in the property which can be transferred or inherited. Nevertheless, such a tenant is not a trespasser either, for neither he nor his predecessor-tenant entered upon the property by wrongful means. In the previous decision a tenant from month to month was thus taken as a synonym of the English "tenant by sufferance". In our law there is no such concept as "tenant by sufferance", who is liable to be evicted at any time and who does not inherit any right in the property. Under the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, a tenant may continue in possession even after lawful termination of his tenancy. A lessee may continue in possession of a lease property on its lawful termination if the landlord either expressly or impliedly recognises him as lessee taking rent from him; he is called a tenant by holding over under section 116 of the TP Act. He is not a tenant by sufferance. Death of the original tenant is not a ground for determining the tenancy, nor a person continuing in possession of the tenancy on the death of the original tenant, as found in that decision, is a trespasser either. In such a circumstance, the only basis of his possession is the right of in her now ever limited in scope that right may be. 

 16. In the instant case, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division accepted the contention of the appellants-tenants that they had not inherited the tenancy from their father, the original tenant, but nevertheless, held them to be "tenants by sufferance" as they were not trespassers. This view is erroneous. 

 17. If a monthly tenancy is found to be heritable a question may arise, whether any difficulty will be faced by landlord if a notice to quit is to be served on several persons who may inherit a tenancy right on the death of their predecessor-tenant. We do not think that any such difficulty will arise. For, on the death of the original tenant several heirs may inherit his right, and all of them become co-tenants or joint tenants. All of them may not be in actual occupation of the premises. A notice under section 106 TP Act must be addressed to all the co-tenants, or joint tenants, but service of the notice upon any one of them must be treated as prima facie service upon them all. If none of them is found in the premises the notice may be served upon "one of his family or servants at the premises". If none of them is found at the premises, the notice may be served by affixing it to any conspicuous part of the premises, as specifically laid down in the second paragraph of section 106. We get support to this view from a number of decisions including the decision of the Privy Council in the case of Harihar Banerji Vs. Ramshasi Roy, AIR 1918 (PC) 102. This decision was followed by us in SM Bindubashini Chanda Vs. Al-haj Jahanara Begum, 1982 BCR (AD) 181. 

 18. In conclusion, we find that a tenancy from month to month is a lease which, like any other lease, is contemplated only in section 105 TP Act and that the right therein is heritable and not personal to vanish with the tenant's death. The right on inheritance is same as that of the original tenant and not in any way better or higher than his right. On re-consideration of the previous decision in 32 DLR (AD) 171 case in the light of the materials now placed before us, we find that that decision is not correct. The Execution Proceeding against the appellants in this case is maintainable. The impugned judgment of the High Court Division is upheld, though on different grounds as given above. The appeal is, therefore, dismissed without, however, any order as to cost.
